name.label: supported
name.says: The name means Hill of Ares, from the Greek Areios Pagos.
quote: translated 'Hill of Ares'

where.label: supported
where.says: The hill is a rocky outcrop northwest of the Acropolis.
quote: a rocky outcrop called the Hill of Ares, northwest of the Acropolis

council.label: supported
council.says: The Areopagus was a principal council of ancient Athens, later mainly a court for homicide and certain religious offences.
quote: was a principal council of ancient Athens, later serving mainly as a judicial body responsible for cases of homicide, wounding, and certain religious offenses

early.label: disputed
early.says: Homicide trials may have been held here as early as the 7th century BC; there is no consensus.
quote: While there is no consensus, homicide trials seem to have been held by Athenians on the Areopagus hill as early as the 7th century BC

ares-myth.label: legend
ares-myth.says: Myth said the god Ares was tried here by the other gods for killing Poseidon's son.
quote: The war god Ares was supposed to have been tried by the other gods on the Areopagus for the murder of Poseidon's son Halirrhothius, a typical example of an aetiological myth.

orestes.label: supported
orestes.says: In Aeschylus's play The Eumenides (458 BC), Orestes is tried here.
quote: In The Eumenides of Aeschylus (458 BC), the Areopagus is the site of the trial of Orestes

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: On a flat spot near the top of the rock, well back from the edges, facing the Acropolis gateway.

paras.t: This bare, rocky hill is the Areopagus. The name means the Hill of Ares, the god of war. In the King James Bible it's Mars' hill.
Watch your footing up here. The rock is uneven, and there are no railings at the edges.

Long before Paul, this rock was famous for justice. The council that met here became the court of Athens for murder and certain religious crimes. Exactly how early that began, historians aren't sure, but it may go back to the 7th century BC.

The Athenians liked a good origin story. Myth said the war god Ares himself was put on trial here by the other gods. And in the play The Eumenides, from 458 BC, the playwright Aeschylus set the trial of Orestes on this hill.

Now to the apostle Paul. The book of Acts, chapter seventeen, tells how the apostle Paul waited in Athens, and his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry. He argued daily in the synagogue, and in the market below us.

Some of the philosophers brought him unto Areopagus, Acts says, to explain his new teaching. Here historians aren't sure what that means: this hill itself, or the council named after it, which by Paul's time probably met down in the marketplace instead. One scholar has even suggested the hearing may have been part lecture, part trial.

Here are his opening words, in the King James Version: "Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, to the unknown god. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you."
Picture saying this in a city Acts describes as wholly given to idolatry: that God that made the world dwelleth not in temples made with hands.
He even quoted their own Greek poets back to them. It was a sermon built for this audience.

parts.name: How it ended
parts.stand: Turn to look down over the Agora.

paras.t: Acts is honest about the result. When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, and others said they would hear him again. But a few believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris.
Paul did not win the crowd that day. But a few people listened, and the words Acts records have been read all over the world ever since.
